hints.title: Check the bound before the integrals
hints.body: A counterexample must keep |f(x)|≤1 throughout the interval but make the proposed integral comparison fail. Sketch the candidates against the bounding strip, then verify their bounds exactly.
hints.recap: A function counterexample must satisfy the assumption at every allowed input.
hints.pitfall: An endpoint that breaks the bound rules a candidate out immediately.
hints.pause: Test the endpoints, then check the full interval for candidates that remain.

recall.reminder: A function counterexample must satisfy the assumption at every allowed input.

hints.title: Factor to check the full-interval bound
hints.body: For a remaining product, bound the size of each factor on the interval. Alternatively, find its largest and smallest values.
hints.recap: Bounds on factors can prove a bound for their product.
hints.pitfall: A few sample values alone do not prove a bound everywhere.
hints.pause: Decide which candidates really satisfy the given assumption.
hints.recallOmissionReason: This step applies a simple product bound to the factors on the stated interval. The catalogue does not explicitly teach that product-bound fact; the body explains it directly rather than claiming a booklet reference.

hints.title: Compare signed area with a squared function
hints.body: For each surviving candidate, compare its values at x and −x. Use any resulting cancellation in its integral, then integrate its square if needed.
hints.recap: Equal and opposite heights cancel in a signed integral.
hints.pitfall: The required failure is a strict reverse inequality; equality is not a counterexample.
hints.pause: Calculate or justify both integrals and select the function that defeats the claim.

recall.reminder: Equal and opposite heights cancel in a signed integral.

solution:
Choose D, f(x)=x−x3. For −1≤x≤1, |f(x)|=|x|(1−x2)≤1, so the full premise holds.

The function is odd, hence its integral over [−1, 1] is 0. Its square equals x2−2x4+x6, whose integral is 23−45+27=16105>0.

Thus ∫f2>∫f, contradicting the claimed inequality while respecting its hypothesis. D is the counterexample.
knowledgePattern: Find an integral-inequality counterexample satisfying its pointwise premise
